__README: SeaweedFS S3 circuit breaker -- per-bucket concurrency and rate caps, returning 429 SlowDown.
It exists because ai-worker-ingestion runs -c 4 and ai-worker-embedding runs -c 2, each child
streaming 64 MiB multipart parts, while Laravel is concurrently streaming uploads and
downloads through PHP-FPM. Without a cap, an ingestion burst saturates the volume server and
the symptom lands on the *interactive* path: a customer's download stalls because a background
job is reindexing. A 429 that a client backs off on is strictly better than a timeout.
<!-- UNVERIFIED --> HOW THIS FILE ACTUALLY REACHES THE GATEWAY
The path /etc/s3/circuit_breaker.json is a path INSIDE THE FILER'S NAMESPACE, not a path on
the container filesystem -- SeaweedFS reads its S3 circuit-breaker configuration from the
filer, unlike -s3.config which is a real file argument. Mounting this file into the container
therefore makes it AVAILABLE but does not ACTIVATE it. It has to be uploaded once, per
cluster, e.g.:
docker compose exec seaweedfs \
weed shell -c "fs.cd /etc/s3" -c "fs.upload /etc/s3/circuit_breaker.json"
Confirm the exact command and the enabled/disabled semantics against the SeaweedFS wiki for
the pinned 4.40 tag before relying on it. Until that upload has run, THE BREAKER IS NOT
ACTIVE -- and unlike the identities file, that is a performance exposure rather than a
security one, so it fails loud (slow) rather than open (unauthenticated).
This file is committed and version-controlled deliberately: it is one of exactly three
SeaweedFS-specific things worth paying for, because all three live entirely in
infrastructure/ (the others are filer.backup/filer.sync and erasure coding for cold volumes).
Migrating to a managed object store deletes these files and changes nothing above the storage
module. That is the whole point of restricting application code to the portable S3 subset.

__comment: Writes are the ingestion path (originals + derived artifacts). 32 concurrent leaves
headroom under the global cap for the interactive read path.
__comment_list: List is capped tightest of all. The deletion verification pass and the abandoned-
multipart sweep both paginate large prefixes, and an unbounded List concurrency is how
a purge job starves the read path it shares a volume server with.

__not_configured_here: LIFECYCLE RULES. SeaweedFS lifecycle needs the admin server plus a lifecycle worker running;
without them a bucket with rules but no worker silently retains data past its declared
expiration, with no error -- and even when it works, the default detection interval is 1440
minutes. Retention here is a PostgreSQL-driven Celery sweep, never a bucket rule.
OBJECT LOCK / LEGAL HOLD. Object Lock requires versioning AND can only be enabled at bucket
creation; there is no retrofit, only a bucket migration. If governance-mode locks for held
originals are ever built, they need a SEPARATE, PRE-CREATED versioned lock-enabled bucket
that held originals are CopyObject'd into. Provision it before it is needed, or the first
legal hold is a bucket migration under time pressure.
SSE-C. filer.backup and filer.sync have no access to customer keys, so SSE-C objects would be
ABSENT from the DR copy. If at-rest encryption is required, use filer-level -encryptVolumeData
(per-chunk AES-256-GCM, keys in filer metadata) -- an ops-layer choice no application code
